thesis: This episode argues that Charlie Munger identifies a specific set of high-quality companies—particularly in consumer brands and technology—that possess durable competitive advantages and pricing power. He emphasizes that these winners, such as Apple, Microsoft, and Costco, are logical candidates for significant portfolio participation, while also noting that some of these stocks were available at attractive valuations when Warren Buffett entered the market.

claims.quote: Andrew: So, there are categories like See’s or Hermes, where brands lead to pricing power…. Charlie: I think your chances of buying one of them are so low, I wouldn't even look.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger mentions Nestle as a company that professional investors buy.
claims.quote: Charlie: There are a lot of professional investors who buy nothing but branded goods. They usually start with this Nestle, and […]. They’ve done two or three points better than average, but it's not a bonanza.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger discusses Kraft Heinz's pricing power, specifically regarding Heinz ketchup vs Kraft cheese.
claims.quote: David: After that, our conversation turned to Kraft Heinz and why Heinz is able to have pricing power while Kraft is not. Charlie: It is very interesting. There’s something about the flavor of ketchup on a goddamned fried potato… that you are really willing to change brands over.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger discusses Apple as a logical candidate for significant participation in the 12 companies that do better than everybody else.
claims.quote: Andrew: Since these guys are very tech-focused, I'm curious about not being a tech person. What did you think about the Apple investment? And what gave you the conviction to be so big? Charlie: What everybody has learned is that everybody needs some significant participation in the 12 companies that do better than everybody else.

claims.quote: Ben: What about other geopolitical considerations? Would you hold TSMC at this point? Charlie: Well I don't like that as well as I like something with a real consumer brand of its own like Apple.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger discusses Costco's business model, culture, and execution, noting its low SKU count and high inventory turnover.
claims.quote: Ben: One Costco question that I've been wanting to ask you is: all the puzzle pieces of the low SKU count, the high inventory turnover… there are just so many things that fit together so beautifully…

claims.claim: Charlie Munger explains that Costco's success is due to culture plus model and reliable execution over 40 years.
claims.quote: Charlie: Yes, culture plus model. Yes, absolutely. And very reliable, hard working, determined execution for 40 years.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger discusses Costco's hotdogs, noting that raising their price would destroy the business.
claims.quote: David: There was no board-level discussion of the hotdog? Charlie: No. Those two would not have thought it was a board matter to discuss the price of the hotdog.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger notes that BYD will sell at least 2.5 million cars this year, most of them electric, which is unheard of.
claims.quote: Charlie: Well BYD, this year will sell at least two and a half million cars. Most of them are electric, that's unheard of. That's way more than Mercedes, for instance.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger states that he invested something like $270 million in BYD, which is now worth something like $8 billion.
claims.quote: Ben: Have you ever had an investment like that before? I think you've invested something like $270 million that's now worth something like $8 billion in BYD.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger describes BYD's founder as a genius with a PhD in engineering who solved all problems on electric cars.
claims.quote: Charlie: The guy was a genius. He had a PhD in engineering, and he look at some great part… [he could make that park look at the morning and look at it. I didn't know he could make it.] I've never seen anybody like that.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger compares BYD's founder to Elon Musk, stating that the BYD founder is better at actually making things.
claims.quote: Charlie: He's a fanatic that knows how to actually make things with his hands if he has to. He's closer to ground zero, in other words. The guy at BYD is better at actually making things than Elon is.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger mentions that BYD sells more cars than Tesla.
claims.quote: David: More than Tesla, right? Charlie: Yeah, more than anybody. Lots of troubles and losses. They ran into terrible trouble. They created the wrong kind… they made lots of mistakes.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger praises Costco for selling cheaper than anyone else in America with efficient stores and a capital-light business model.
claims.quote: They really did sell cheaper than anybody else in America and they did it in big, efficient stores. The parking spaces were 10 feet wide instead of eight or nine feet or whatever they normally are.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger highlights Costco's capital-light business model where they have no investment in inventory and suppliers carry the inventory until sold.
claims.quote: They have no investment in inventory. They make the suppliers wait until they've been paid and then they're scheduled to pay only after they're scheduled to sell.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger describes Costco as one of the few great companies in a lifetime that you should bet big on because it works wonderfully.
claims.quote: There aren't many times in a lifetime when you know you're right and you know you have one that's really going to work wonderfully. Maybe five or six times in a lifetime you get a chance to do it.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger mentions Gelson Brothers as a little grocery store chain in Los Angeles that wanted high turnovers and low capital costs but never made money.
claims.quote: That little grocery store chain here in Los Angeles, Gelson Brothers. They wanted the high turnovers and low capital costs, and they never made the least effort to earn any money.

claims.claim: Charlie Munger believes it is good for the world to have an independent store of value like Bitcoin that is not pegged to a nation state.
claims.quote: Of course, it's good to the world as a whole to have a way of having some currency. The way that was solved is for a long time, the British pound was the national currency of the investment world.
